0.1.n: A very familiar, rough way to address someone, fitting this blunt scolding.

0.2.n: Drawn-out な adds emphasis while calling for the listener's attention.

0.4.n: Together with か, 何 forms an unspecified thing rather than a question.

0.5.n: Attached to 何, it makes 何か instead of asking what.

0.6.n: する changes to したい to express a desire to act.

0.8.n: This repeated 何か echoes the listener's constant talk about taking action.

0.9.n: Combines with 何 to avoid naming any particular activity.

0.10.n: Repeating したい makes the listener's stated desire sound tiresome.

0.11.n: Casually marks the repeated words as a quotation, with the verb for saying left out.

0.13.n: Adds impatience here rather than simply marking something as already done.

0.14.n: Literally mouth; with ばっかり, it contrasts words with action.

0.15.n: An emphatic conversational version of ばかり, restricting the person's behavior to talk.

0.16.n: Part of Kansai-style やんけ, forcefully pointing out something the speaker considers obvious.

0.17.n: Completes やんけ, giving the criticism a rough, confrontational tone rather than asking a genuine question.

1.0.n: A Kansai dialect word corresponding to standard Japanese 本当.

1.1.n: Turns ほんま into ほんまに, which describes how sincerely the person wants to change.

1.2.n: 変わる becomes 変わりたい, then 変わりたかったら to express a condition, not a past desire.

1.3.n: Drawn-out な keeps the listener engaged while emphasizing the condition.

2.0.n: Combines with でも to allow any activity, without specifying one.

2.1.n: After 何, でも means there is no restriction on the choice.

2.2.n: Kansai dialect equivalent of いい, accepting any choice of action.

2.3.n: Gives the reason for the command: any activity is acceptable.

2.5.n: The speaker addresses the listener directly again, maintaining a rough, familiar tone.

2.7.n: This segment begins 行動せえ, the Kansai-style command corresponding to 行動しろ.

2.8.n: Completes せえ; it belongs to the command form of する, not a separate word.

2.9.n: Strengthens the command and pushes the listener to act.

3.0.n: Marks the preceding speech as what the narrator was told.

3.1.n: 言う becomes passive 言われる, then polite linking 言われまして, connecting the experience to what follows.

3.3.n: Points back to the advice just quoted.

3.4.n: Refers collectively to the brother's message, not just one individual word.

3.5.n: Identifies the brother's words as what had an emotional impact.

3.6.n: The describing form of すごい strengthens the emotional effect of 響いて.

3.7.n: The linking て-form of 響く describes emotional impact here, rather than a sound echoing.

4.0.n: Marks this as the narrator's first genuine decision to do something.

4.1.n: Combines with か to refer to an unspecified activity.

4.2.n: Makes 何 indefinite rather than a question about what to do.

4.3.n: Marks 何か as the thing the narrator intends to do.

4.4.n: The intention form of する expresses the narrator's resolve within the quoted thought.

4.5.n: Casually marks 何かをしよう as the content of the narrator's thought.

4.7.n: Combines with 3年生 to identify the narrator's stage of education.

4.8.n: 年生 identifies a student's school year, not their age.

4.9.n: Links 大学3年生 to 時, describing which period of life is meant.

4.10.n: With 大学3年生の, it refers to the period when the narrator was a third-year college student.

4.11.n: Marks that period as when the thought occurred.

4.12.n: The て-form of 思う links this realization to the next event in the story.

5.0.n: Moves the story forward from the decision to the conversation.

5.1.n: A typically masculine self-reference, softer and less rough than 俺.

5.2.n: Sets the narrator as the person the sentence is about.

5.3.n: Used for one's own older brother when talking to others.

5.4.n: Marks the brother as the recipient of the narrator's words.

5.5.n: The polite past form of 言う appears in the narration, outside the casual quotation.

6.1.n: An energetic, casual exclamation showing determination or readiness.

6.2.n: The plain past form of 分かる signals understanding and acceptance here.

6.4.n: A casual shortening of では, introducing the plan that follows from the advice.

6.5.n: A strongly casual, typically masculine self-reference used when speaking to someone close.

6.7.n: Expresses a repeated daily schedule without needing a particle.

6.8.n: 時 marks a clock time; 毎朝 makes clear that this is in the morning.

6.9.n: Marks six o'clock as the starting time of the activity.

6.10.n: A station name combining the place name 新宿 with 駅, meaning station.

6.11.n: Marks the location where the trash-picking activity will happen.

6.12.n: Combines directly with 拾い to name the cleanup activity.

6.13.n: The noun-like form of 拾う combines with ゴミ to form ゴミ拾い.

6.14.n: Turns ゴミ拾い into an action; the plain nonpast form expresses a future commitment here.

7.0.n: Casually marks the preceding promise as the words the narrator said.

7.1.n: The plain past form of 言う directly describes 言葉: the words the narrator said.

7.2.n: Refers to the narrator's whole promise about picking up trash.

7.3.n: Treats the narrator's statement as what the brother's reply addresses.

7.5.n: Refers again to the narrator's own older sibling.

7.6.n: Identifies the brother as the person who responded.

7.7.n: Points forward to the exact reply quoted next.

7.8.n: The polite past form of 返す means giving a verbal response here, not returning an object.

8.1.n: A casual question asking the reason for the narrator's proposed activity.

0.lit: You, listen, want to do something, want to do something, saying that—honestly, nothing but talk, aren't you!
0.tip: 口ばっかり means all talk, and Kansai-style やんけ makes the criticism rough and emphatic.

1.lit: If you really want to change, you know,
1.tip: Despite its past-looking shape, たかったら means if you want to, not if you wanted to in the past.

2.lit: Anything is fine, so you, take action!
2.tip: せえ is a Kansai-style command form of する, equivalent to standard しろ.

3.lit: I was told that, and those words resonated deeply,
3.tip: 言われまして presents the narrator as receiving the advice and politely links it to the next part.

4.lit: For the first time, I'll do something, I thought during my third year of college,
4.tip: しようって思って quotes a personal intention: the narrator decided to do something.

5.lit: And then I said to my older brother.
5.tip: に marks the person being spoken to after a verb like 言う.

6.lit: Alright, understood; then I, every morning from six, at Shinjuku Station, will do trash picking!
6.tip: から marks the starting time, while で marks where the activity takes place.

7.lit: In response to the words I said, my older brother replied like this.
7.tip: こう points forward to the exact words of the brother's reply.

8.tip: 何で asks for a reason here, not a means or method.
